rationale: *Priestia aryabhattai* (Bacillaceae) by ANI. **The "Aneurinibacillus, 100% genus support" label carried here since pool v2 was wrong**, and the reason is worth recording: MEGAN percentages are normalised within each rank row, so a row holding a single name always reads 100% however few reads back it. This genome's own family row says Bacillaceae 99.98% against Aneurinibacillaceae 0.02%, and its order row says Bacillales 99.96% — the genus row was the outlier, not the evidence. ANI is decisive: zero hits across all 436 Paenibacillaceae species, against *P. aryabhattai* at 99.47% in Bacillaceae. identify_strains.py now reads the family row directly and escalates there when it disagrees with the genus. The keystone: L-lactate producer-favoured with annotated export, zero predicted requirements, catalase-positive, zero lactate consumption, and a confident DHA kinase so it can also act as receiver. Covers biotin, pantothenate and respiratory quinone for partners. Not a risk genus.

Bacillus, 99.38%. Best aerobic profile in the pool: four PDH subunits but no pyruvate oxidase and no NADH oxidase, so least pyruvate and NADH diverted from lactate under aeration. Prototrophic, L-only, annotated export.
Bacillus, 100%. Equal producer score to P1_B11 but requires biotin, which makes it the test case for biotin rescue by P1_B3 or P3_G9. Also a DHA receiver.

Paenibacillus, 100%. Producer-favoured and prototrophic but carries no annotated lactate transporter, and its GEM correspondingly has no lactate exchange. Tests whether the unannotated-export call predicts a real inability to secrete.

Gluconobacter frateurii by ANI (96.7%, 90% aligned) — not G. oxydans. Membrane-bound PQQ sldAB with four pqq genes, so glycerol is oxidised in the periplasm and DHA appears extracellularly without a transporter. Complete aerobic cob* route, so it is also the pool's B12 source. Requires methionine, pantothenate, quinone.
Gluconobacter, 99.86%. Same periplasmic PQQ signature but a genuinely distinct genome, unlike P3_H7 which carves identically to P3_C11.

Lactococcus lactis by ANI (98.2%). Loses every role under aeration — noxE, poxL, no catalase, heme-dependent, lipoate salvage-only, eight requirements, unannotated export — yet it is the food-grade industrial lactate organism. Included because it is the one strain where a community could plausibly beat the monoculture: heme and catalase from a partner plus a lipoate-free medium to suppress PDH.
Rahnella, 99.90%. Highest provision count available at 22 pathways with catalase, but it consumes lactate. Tests directly whether nutritional richness is worth the product loss.

Lysinibacillus xylanilyticus by ANI (96.0%, 89% aligned), genus 99.99% with a consistent Planococcaceae family call. Three lactate consumption genes and no L-LDH, so it is a product sink; prototrophic, catalase-positive, and grows on glycerol. Chosen over the alternatives for the *fewest* provisions in the pool (13), which is what a clean sink control needs — P2_D5 (Pantoea) offered 22 and would have confounded the sink effect with nutritional support. Replaces P1_G5, which ANI identified as Brucella pseudogrignonensis (99.56%, strain-level) — an opportunistic pathogen that the screen had cleared because Ochrobactrum predates its 2020 reclassification into Brucella. P3_E12 (Pseudochrobactrum) was rejected for the same reason: Rhizobiaceae, with Ochrobactrum among its nearest genus neighbours.

Lactiplantibacillus, 99.98%. The highest-value addition available, for a reason that comes straight out of OVERFLOW_TRIGGERS.md: *L. plantarum* LDH is the documented **FBP-independent** bacterial L-LDH, where Bacillus and Lactococcus LDHs need fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to activate. Glycerol enters glycolysis below the aldolase step, so FBP is a gluconeogenic trickle — hypothesis H3 says that should cripple FBP-dependent producers on glycerol. This strain is the direct test of that, and it is food-grade with decades of process literature, which the three current producers entirely lack. Six L-LDH and two D-LDH copies, producer-favoured, annotated export. Eleven requirements including heme, biotin and quinone, so it is also the pool's strongest beneficiary of the supporters. Risk to be aware of: no cytoplasmic glycerol dehydrogenase, so it may not grow on glycerol alone at all — which the viability gate will settle, and which is informative either way.

Leuconostoc, 99.02%. Heterofermentative LAB — D-lactate dominant (4 D-LDH to 1 L-LDH) plus ethanol and CO2, a fermentation mode absent from the pool. Has no glycerol kinase, so it cannot start on the feedstock and can only live on cross-fed carbon. That is not a defect for this brief: an obligate cross-feeder is precisely the kind of member whose behaviour is not predictable from its own genome, and it tests whether the pool generates enough exchangeable carbon to carry a passenger. Catalase-negative, so it shares P3_B12's need for a peroxide scavenger.

Staphylococcus, 99.78% — **conditional on species-level ANI, run before the model is built.** Highest producer score in the entire 384-genome screen (43.8), L-and-D, producer-favoured, annotated export, and consumes no lactate. Many environmental staphylococci are BSL-1 and two (*S. xylosus*, *S. equorum*) are food-fermentation organisms; *S. aureus* is the exclusion. Zero virulence name matches, flagged only for genus membership. Requires proline, serine and biotin, all covered in-pool. Drop on an *aureus*-group call.

BIGb0383, 99.88% — an unresolved genus label, so ANI is genuinely informative here rather than confirmatory. Nine annotated amino-acid exporters, the most in the library, with 22 provided pathways and no requirements. Uniquely among the supporters it has **no pyruvate oxidase and no NADH oxidase**, so it diverts nothing from the lactate node, and it carries annotated lactate export with catalase, peroxidase and superoxide dismutase. The closest thing to a free supporter in the pool.

Ewingella, 99.97%. Joint-highest provisioner at 23 pathways with seven amino-acid exporters, and the best oxidative defence available — catalase 3, peroxidase 4, superoxide dismutase 2. That matters specifically for P3_B12, P2_A5 and P1_F12, which are catalase-poor and heme-dependent; LITERATURE_CROSSREF.md established that peroxide load, not nutrition, is what caps Lactococcus aerobically on glycerol. Consumes lactate but has no annotated exporter, so it is a value-adding consumer rather than a cycling one.

Erwinia, 99.70%. 23 provided pathways and six amino-acid exporters, plus five pqq genes — so it is a second, phylogenetically independent DHA donor alongside the two Gluconobacters, which are near-duplicates of each other. Breaks the pool's single point of failure on the DHA route.

Pantoea, 100%. 22 provided pathways, six amino-acid exporters, five pqq genes and strong oxidative defence. Previously *rejected* as a sink control because 22 provisions would have confounded the sink effect with nutritional support — under the new brief that is exactly the property wanted, so the earlier rejection reverses.

Rhodococcus, 99.48%. Actinobacteria — a phylum absent from the pool. Twenty provided pathways, six amino-acid exporters, catalase 3, no requirements, and a 7.5 Mbp genome with unusually broad catabolic range. Seven PDH subunits means a large pyruvate drain, so it is not a producer; it is here for robustness and for interactions nothing in the annotation predicts. Assembly is 'acceptable' rather than good at 157 contigs.

Oerskovia, 99.62%. Second Actinobacterium, chosen over Corynebacterium and Leucobacter for one decisive reason: it grows on glycerol and **consumes no lactate**. Corynebacterium P2_B2 was the obvious pick on paper — the classic amino-acid overproducer genus, catalase 3, 18 pathways — but it has neither glycerol kinase nor facilitator and five lactate-consumption genes, making it a pure product sink that cannot even use the feedstock. Nineteen provided pathways; needs biotin, which is covered in-pool.

Chryseobacterium, 99.95%. Bacteroidetes — a third phylum. Carries a **periplasmic** glycerol dehydrogenase plus two cytoplasmic ones, so it is a third independent DHA donor by a different mechanism than the PQQ quinoproteins. Consumes no lactate, 18 provided pathways, requires only proline. The most functionally distinct member of the additions.

Chishuiella, 100% genus support. **The only other genome in 384 that is genuinely inert toward lactate**: zero L-LDH, zero D-LDH, zero lldD/dld, and zero lactate transporter, all confirmed by direct KO check rather than score column. It can neither contaminate the product nor consume it. Carries glpK and glpF so it can establish on the feedstock rather than needing to be carried, and has a **periplasmic glycerol dehydrogenase**, making it a third independent DHA-donor mechanism alongside the Gluconobacter quinoproteins and P2_E7. Fifteen provided pathways but **zero annotated amino-acid exporters**, so it provisions cofactors rather than amino acids -- pair it with a tier-B strain rather than relying on it alone. Bacteroidetes, needs proline, biotin and thiamine, all covered in-pool.

Brevibacterium, 99.8%. Purity-safe by the hard filter -- zero L-LDH and zero D-LDH confirmed by KO check -- with 18 provided pathways, 3 amino-acid exporters and catalase 2. Requires **only biotin**, the lightest dependency of any candidate at this provisioning level, and it is covered by eight pool members. Actinobacteria, so phylogenetically distant from the producers. The cost is explicit: two lldD/dld copies and three lactate transporters, so it will eat L-lactate. That is a titre penalty to be measured, not a specification failure.

Leucobacter, 99.8%. **Five annotated amino-acid exporters, the most of any purity-safe candidate without a biosafety flag** -- Lelliottia P3_G2 has seven but is Enterobacteriaceae with an hlyC match, which is the family and the flag pattern this whole exercise is trying to avoid. Eighteen provided pathways, Actinobacteria, zero LDH of either isomer. Also eats lactate (2 lldD/dld). Directly addresses the gap P2_G8 leaves: this is the amino-acid provider for the purity-constrained arm, and the H5 precursor-supply hypothesis needs one. Requires sulfate assimilation, biotin and thiamine (salvage).

Paenibacillus, 100%. The cleanest genuinely new option: 18 provided pathways, two L-LDH and **zero** D-LDH and zero lactate oxidase, so it can contribute L-lactate but never contaminate or consume. Requires only biotin, which eight pool members supply. Carries `glpK` but **no `glpF`** — as do all four qualifying Paenibacillus, so glycerol uptake for that genus is the open question and the model gate decides it.

Paenibacillus, 100%. **The best supporter profile in the entire qualifying set** — 19 provided pathways, catalase 3 (the strongest oxidative shield among clean candidates), **zero requirements**, L-only, no consumption. Re-added deliberately after being cut in pool v2 for the one thing that has not changed: **it cannot use glycerol.** `GLYCtex` delivers glycerol to the periplasm and `GLYK` waits in the cytosol with no inner-membrane transport between them, and the genome has no `glpF` or any MIP-family aquaglyceroporin. So it is an obligate cross-feeder. Included because the purity constraint makes provisioning scarce enough that a strain which cannot touch the feedstock but shields the LAB from peroxide is worth testing — and because whether the pool releases enough exchangeable carbon to carry a passenger is itself one of the more interesting questions in the design.

Oerskovia merdavium, 99.6%. **The only clean qualifier with both `glpK` and `glpF`**, so the only one certain to establish on the feedstock unaided, at 19 provided pathways. Re-added with an explicit caveat: its model **fails the redox gate** at electron recovery 1.0714, and unlike `P1_A3` the leak does not localise — the per-reaction imbalances cancel, so it runs through a metabolite whose formula cannot be scored. Treat its quantitative output as unreliable; it is usable for presence/absence coexistence and provisioning tests, not for yield numbers. The strain is very likely fine — the reconstruction is not.
